title: Coarse cloth, jade inside
hook: the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside (Tao Te Ching 70)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a foot back: better to give up a foot than push forward an inch. Your line was a foot back. Did you step back from anything? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A plain wool coat, a little frayed at the cuff. Nobody on the bus looks at it twice. Sewn into the lining, out of sight, is a small stone worth more than everything else the wearer owns. The coat isn't a disguise. It's just a coat. What matters is simply somewhere else. Chapter seventy of the Tao Te Ching ends on a picture very like that, and it gets there by way of a complaint.
screen: `A PLAIN COAT.` → `SOMETHING SEWN INSIDE.` → `THE CHAPTER'S COMPLAINT.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. The speaker says: my words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, and yet nobody in the world understands them or practices them. That's a strange thing for a book to admit about itself. The teaching is simple, and it still goes unused. Second, the reason. The chapter says words have an ancestor and deeds have a master, something they come from. People who don't know that root, it says, don't know me either. Those who know me are few, and that makes what I carry precious. Third, the picture. So the sage wears coarse cloth, the rough garment of a laborer, and holds jade at the breast. In the picture, the precious stone rides close to the body, under cheap, rough fabric. Notice what the chapter doesn't say. It doesn't say the sage hides the jade out of fear, or shows it off to the right people. It just says the outside is plain and the inside is precious, and the two don't have to match. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Some of what's most valuable in a life doesn't photograph well. A promise kept for years. A habit of noticing who's left out. A sentence someone said to you once that still steadies you. None of it needs a better coat. And a treasure that's always on display can start to be about the display. The question it leaves: what's your jade, and does it need anyone's eyes on it?
screen: `EASY WORDS, RARELY USED.` · `FEW KNOW THE ROOT.` · `PLAIN OUTSIDE, JADE INSIDE.` · `WHAT'S YOUR JADE?` · then, large: `COARSE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one treasure hidden. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Then ask, quietly: what's one good thing in my life I don't need to announce? A kindness you're doing. Something you're learning. A thing you love that nobody else much cares about. Let it come to mind and stay with it. Feel what it's like to hold it without telling anyone, the way the sage holds jade under a rough coat. If the urge to share it rises, notice the urge and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
Coarse cloth. Chapter seventy's picture of the sage: rough, plain clothing outside, precious jade carried close inside. Today's word.
Your line: jade inside. Today, do one good thing and tell no one. Let it stay under the coat. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy's image of the sage, plain cloth outside and jade inside, as a picture of a life whose real worth is carried quietly rather than displayed.

pairs: easy to know, easy to practice

myth: chapter seventy says its teaching is too hard for most people
it says the words are very easy to understand and practice, yet nobody does.
the sage in chapter seventy wears rough cloth and carries jade inside

it gives no such reason. it simply sets the plain outside beside the precious inside.

fork.setup: you carry something precious. chapter seventy pictures how the sage dresses. what does the sage wear?
options: fine silk to match the jade.
coarse cloth, with the jade held inside.
nothing special, and leaves the jade at home.
fork.reveal: the sage wears coarse cloth and holds jade at the breast. the outside doesn't have to advertise the inside.

original.note: Chinese: wearing coarse cloth, holding jade at the breast, from chapter seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: coarse cloth is about dressing down.
what it means: what's most precious can be carried quietly, under a plain outside.
what a scholar hears: the line comes right after the complaint that the words are easy yet unknown, so the jade is also the teaching itself.

notes: Chapter 70 is paraphrased throughout; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording.
褐 (hè) is glossed as the rough garment of a laborer; confirm the gloss.
The trapdoor's third floor (the jade as the teaching itself) is one reading of the chapter's structure; confirm it is fair.
Original 被褐懷玉 (pī hè huái yù) rendered 'PEE huh HWAI yoo'. Confirm.
